newsitem.title: UK: Britain elects record number of women legislators.
newsitem.headline: Britain elects record number of women legislators.

text.p: A record number of women will take up seats in the "Mother of Parliaments" after the Labour Party made its best ever showing in Britain's general election.
As results trickled in on Friday, the number of female members of parliament (MPs) looked set to double from 62 to about 120, although Westminster will remain overwhelmingly male.
"I'm pleased that there will be a real mix of MPs, with more women and younger Members of Parliament," said Claire Ward, who at 24 became the youngest member of the current intake.
Twin sisters Angela and Maria Eagle were also swept to Westminster on the tidal wave of support for Labour, becoming both the first twins and the first sisters to enter parliament.
Nearly 400 women had run for parliament's 659 seats in Thursday's election and their one-in-four success rate means the magic 100 mark will be broken for the first time.

"It will be important that a number of women are all entering at the same time. If there is a huge chunk of women all new together, it will be easier to back each other up," said analyst Mary-Ann Stephenson of the Fawcett Society.

Labour, on course for a majority of close to 180 seats, had 101 of the 1997 intake, with the Conservatives, traditionally favoured by women voters, supplying 12. Others came from the Scottish National Party and the Liberal Democrats.

Before Thursday's election, women made up just 9.2 percent of the House of Commons and analysts said the scale of the new influx should finally make a difference to the way business is conducted at Westminster.
Currently, the corridors of power resemble a boys' school or a gentlemen's club more than a modern parliamentary democracy.
Women's toilets are notoriously hard to find.
There is a rifle range and 11 bars, but no creche.

Pressure is building to convert the in-house barber into a women-friendly salon and, most importantly, men are being urged to tone down their confrontational debating rhetoric and adopt a more inclusive, positive tone in the chamber.
Clare Short, Labour's most popular woman MP, has long attacked the boys' school atmosphere and lamented the fact that she was one of only 187 women MPs ever elected in Britain.
"Sometimes I feel embarrassed to be there. I hope my Mum isn't watching," Short said of the barracking that often passes for political debate in parliament.

"As women are pushing forward in workplaces and all the professions...the House of Commons looks odder and odder, with rows and rows of men in suits talking and behaving in ways that would not be respected or tolerated in the real world."
A long-time champion of women's rights, Labour has promised to ensure that half of all MPs are female within 10 years.
But despite the latest gains, the profile of women in British politics is still low when comparisons are drawn with Europe, Asia and the United States.
In Germany, about one in four MPs are women.
Norway and Sweden both introduced quota systems that led to governments comprising an equal mix of men and women.
And from Iceland to Ireland, voters have picked women presidents whereas former prime minister Margaret Thatcher was referred to as "the only man in the cabinet" during her tenure.
